'Naveen, where's the test report? I asked for it an hour ago.'
'Farhan, I'm on it, the server was down—'
'Everything's always down.'
Naveen went quiet. Across the desk, Meenal stopped typing. Somebody's chair creaked. Farhan looked round the small office: three faces, all tight, the same way his own felt.
'Hold on.' He breathed out slowly. 'Sorry, Naveen. That was me being stressed, not you being slow.'
'It's okay.'
'It isn't, really. Listen, all of you. The client moved the deadline to Thursday and I'm worried. I've been snapping since morning.'
'We figured,' said Meenal, half smiling.
'Right. Let's see what's actually left. Naveen, how long for the report once the server's up?'
'Two hours, maybe.'
'Good. Meenal, the screens?'
'Nearly done.'
'Then we can make Thursday.' Naveen's shoulders came down. Someone went to make tea for everyone.

qa.a: He breathed out, apologised to Naveen, admitted he was worried about the deadline and turned to what was left, and the team relaxed.

qa.a: Naveen probably felt blamed and hurt, going quiet, and then relieved when Farhan said it was his stress, not Naveen being slow.

subtype: Setting the tone of a team [Response]
passage: The kitchen at the hotel goes quiet in a particular way when the head of the line is in a bad mood. I learned that last winter. I was twenty-four, new to running the evening line, and scared of every order. So I barked. On one busy Friday Saurabh dropped a stack of plates right after I snapped at him, and the young cook beside him burned the onions. Later, washing up, Saurabh said, 'Sonali di, when you're tense, we all go tense. We're watching your face.' That stung. It was also true. Now, before service, I stand at the pass, take one slow breath and say something honest: 'Big night, we're short one person, we'll get through it.' I still feel the pressure. I just stopped throwing it at them. The plates break less now. Mostly.

qa.a: Saurabh dropped a stack of plates right after Sonali snapped at him.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when Saurabh said the team watched her face?
qa.a: It stung, but Sonali also recognised it was true, which made her rethink how her mood affected the line.

qa.q: What does Sonali do now before service, and why does it help?
qa.a: She takes one slow breath at the pass and says something honest about the pressure, so the team hears calm instead of catching her stress.

qa.q: If you were the young cook on the line, what would you notice about the change?
qa.a: You would likely feel less jumpy and more able to focus, since the head of the line is steady and honest instead of barking.

grounding: A young kitchen lead recalls learning that her tension spread through the line, and now breathes before service and names the pressure calmly.

Supervisor's note, Mohit, call centre floor 3, end of quarter:
Divyansh, our youngest team lead, had a rough first month. On bad days he paced, sighed loudly and sent sharp messages, and I watched his team's call times get longer and their faces tighter. In week five I mentioned it once. Since then I've seen a clear change. Before the morning huddle he stands by the window for a minute, then starts with the honest version: 'Targets are tough this week, I feel it too. Here's the plan.' When a call goes badly, he speaks quietly and asks what happened. The team now jokes during breaks again, and two of them told me they feel 'less on edge'. Next step: I've asked Divyansh to share how he does it at the new leads' training on Monday.

qa.q: What does Divyansh do before the morning huddle now?
qa.a: He stands by the window for a minute, then starts with the honest version of how the week looks.

qa.q: How can you tell Divyansh's team felt his stress in the first month?
qa.a: Their call times got longer and their faces tighter when he paced, sighed loudly and sent sharp messages.

qa.q: Which change in Divyansh's habits made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Pausing before the huddle and admitting the targets were tough in a calm voice gave the team a steady person to follow instead of a tense one.

qa.q: How might the team members experience their workday now?
qa.a: They seem more relaxed and able to joke again, and two said they feel less on edge, so the floor is easier to work on.

Tuesday, late
Today I watched my own mood walk around the studio. At the ten o'clock stand-up I was already snapping: "Why isn't scene 12 rendered?" Jasleen went quiet. By lunch two animators were arguing over a shared file, and someone slammed a drawer. Nobody had yelled at them. I had just been sighing at everything for three days, and they'd caught it.
So at the four o'clock check-in I tried something. Before walking in, I stood by the water cooler and breathed out slowly, three times. Then I said, "Honestly, the client deadline scares me too. We're behind. Let's pick the three scenes that matter most." Jasleen actually laughed. The room loosened. We made a list.
Note to self: they read my face more than my slides.
Jatin

qa.a: Jasleen went quiet under the snapping, probably feeling blamed and tense, which makes Jasleen's laugh at four o'clock a real sign of relief.
